title: Maker's Schedule, Manager's Schedule: why meetings cost makers half a day
summary: Paul Graham distinguishes the manager's schedule (one-hour slots) from the maker's schedule (half-day blocks at least). A single meeting can wreck a maker's afternoon and even the morning before it. He explains how Y Combinator copes with office hours clustered at the end of the day, and why speculative meetings are only cheap for managers.

principles.text: Makers need half-day blocks; hour slots are barely enough to get started on hard work.
principles.quote: You can't write or program well in units of an hour. That's barely enough time to get started.

principles.text: One meeting can wreck a maker's whole afternoon by splitting it into pieces too small for hard work.
principles.quote: A single meeting can blow a whole afternoon, by breaking it into two pieces each too small to do anything hard in.

principles.text: Anticipated interruptions lower morale and discourage ambitious projects, which sit near the limit of your capacity.
principles.quote: ambitious projects are by definition close to the limits of your capacity. A small decrease in morale is enough to kill them off.

principles.text: Cluster unavoidable meetings at the end of the day using office hours, so they compress the day but never interrupt it.
principles.quote: By using the classic device for simulating the manager's schedule within the maker's: office hours.

principles.text: Split the day into a maker half and a manager half, protecting deep work from interruption.
principles.quote: in effect I had two workdays each day, one on the manager's schedule and one on the maker's.

principles.text: Speculative meetings like grabbing coffee are free for managers but very costly for makers.
principles.quote: Speculative meetings are terribly costly if you're on the maker's schedule, though.
